summary:
Tambov Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where the legal and physical risks for transgender visitors are severe and have deepened since 2022. The 2023 law signed by Vladimir Putin prohibits gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents, and the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records that trans-specific healthcare has effectively been banned since that year, alongside a ban on same-sex marriage and an absence of discrimination protection.

The Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and convictions followed quickly. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in that movement or for displaying its symbols, comprising 98 administrative and 3 criminal cases; at least 20 people faced criminal charges from January 2024 onward, and three publishing-house staff charged on 15 May 2025 face up to 12 years in prison. Repeated display of banned symbols carries up to four years.

The expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that, explicitly, "justifies" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and national government advisories state this directly: the US State Department rates travel to Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Under the UK Home Office standard, LGB people are not assessed as generally at real risk of persecution solely for their sexual orientation, while trans people, people in the North Caucasus and public LGBT advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. A transgender visitor therefore falls within the category that authority treats as facing a real risk, wherever in Russia they enter.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented at the national level. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement volume has escalated alongside severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, with fines under those statutes bringing more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The post-designation crackdown moved within hours. The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024 that, within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Detainee deaths have been recorded in extremism-related custody. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Human Rights Watch's 30 June 2025 tally counted charges brought under both the administrative and criminal codes, and the organisation called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025).

The UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
localsOnly:
Residents of Tambov Oblast cannot obtain legal recognition of their gender on Russian official documents, and the route to gender-affirming surgery has been closed since 2023; the UK Home Office characterises trans-specific healthcare as effectively banned for the whole country.

No discrimination protection on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation exists in Russian law, and same-sex marriage is prohibited, so residents have no domestic remedy for refusal of service, employment or housing.

The UK Home Office reported that 139 people were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024, a national aggregate that the note does not break down by region.

Residents who display symbols associated with the designated "international LGBT movement" face up to four years in prison on repetition, and up to 12 years for the most serious participation charges, as applied to the three publishing-house staff charged on 15 May 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
The UK Home Office country policy note contains no Tambov Oblast-specific findings; its assessment of risk to trans people is stated at the national level, and no source in this inventory documents enforcement activity, raids or arrests by Tambov Oblast police.

Whether Tambov Oblast courts have issued extremism-related convictions, and how many of the 101 convictions recorded by Human Rights Watch were entered in this oblast, is not sourced. The oblast-level distribution of the 139 people affected by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 also remains unresolved.

No source here records whether a foreign transgender traveller entering Tambov Oblast has been stopped, screened or denied entry on gender-marker grounds; the entry and screening risk described derives from national advisory language rather than documented cases in this oblast.
